title: The Shōgun's Edo
subtitle: In the Floating World, Every Lantern Hides a Knife 🏮⚔️

setting.name: Edo, the Shōgun's Castle Town
setting.description: Edo is the beating heart of the realm — a sprawling castle town of a million souls crouched in the shadow of the warlord's black-and-gold keep. Wooden townhouses lean shoulder to shoulder along canals that reek of brine and incense, fishmongers bellow over mountains of silver tuna at dawn, and pilgrims throng a great temple whose vermilion gate is hung with a lantern the size of an ox. Beneath the lantern-light and the smell of grilled eel, a quieter war is fought in whispers: shinobi clans, merchant cartels, and the shōgun's spymasters trade secrets and steel in the dark. The city is called part of the ukiyo — the Floating World — a place of fleeting pleasure and fleeting loyalty, where a courtesan's smile and an assassin's blade cost roughly the same.
setting.atmosphere: Lantern-glow on wet timber. The rhythmic clack of geta sandals on bridge planks. Smoke from a thousand cookfires hazing the rooftops gold at sunset and grey at dawn. The city is loud, fragrant, and beautiful — and underneath the festival drums there is a held breath, a sense that something is being moved into position just out of sight. Paper walls mean no conversation is ever truly private. By night the merry districts blaze with red lanterns and laughter; by the same light, figures in dark cloth run the rooftops, and a careful traveler learns that in Edo the most dangerous people bow the lowest. 🏯

keyLocations.name: Senkō-ji Temple and the Lantern Gate
keyLocations.description: The spiritual heart of the Asakura district: a towering temple complex approached through the Kaminari-mon, a great vermilion gate from which hangs a single colossal red paper lantern, taller than a man, its base painted with a coiling black dragon. Beyond the gate runs a long, narrow shopping street roofed against the rain and packed cheek-to-jowl with stalls selling rice crackers, folding fans, carved combs, grilled mochi, and lucky charms. The street ends at the temple's incense cauldron, where pilgrims waft sacred smoke over their heads for health, and a second inner gate guarded by two snarling wooden guardian kings opens onto the main hall.
features: The Kaminari-mon gate and its giant red lantern, which sways and creaks in the wind and can be climbed (Athletics DC 14) for a vantage over the whole approach
The covered shopping street — roughly ninety stalls, a riot of color, noise, and crowd cover ideal for losing or catching a tail
A great bronze incense cauldron wreathed in fragrant smoke; the temple's monks read fortunes on slips of paper drawn from numbered drawers
The inner sanctuary with its gilded altar, where the head priest Genshō receives petitioners behind a screen
encounters: A pickpocket child bumps a party member and lifts a purse — or plants a folded message into their sleeve
A fortune-slip drawn at the cauldron reads as a coded warning that someone is watching the party
A hooded informant signals the party to follow them into the crowd, with a rival shinobi shadowing from the rooftops
secrets: The head priest Genshō is a reluctant courier for the conspiracy, blackmailed into passing counterfeit seals hidden inside fortune-slip drawers
A loose floor plank beneath the altar conceals a strongbox of forged tax-seals stamped with the shōgun's own crest

keyLocations.name: The Dawn Fish Market (Uogashi)
keyLocations.description: Before the sun clears the rooftops, the riverside fish market roars to life — a labyrinth of dripping stalls, sloshing tubs, and torch-lit auction pits where whole tuna the size of a grown man are slapped onto cypress blocks and carved with blades as long as an arm. Buyers ring hand-bells, auctioneers chant prices in a sing-song no outsider can follow, and porters sprint through the throng balancing crates, shouting for room. The stone floor is slick with ice-melt and fish blood, and the whole place smells of salt, cedar, and money. 🐟
features: The auction pits, where the day's great tuna are sold at a frantic, coded chant
Narrow aisles between stalls — perfect for a foot chase, full of obstacles, hanging nets, and stacked crates
A maze of back-channels where flat-bottomed boats unload the night's catch and other, quieter cargo
Mountains of crushed ice and stacked barrels that can be toppled for cover or to block pursuit
encounters: A chase scene: an informant or fleeing forger bolts through the market, the party in pursuit across slick stone and toppling crates
A 'fishmonger' who is really a shinobi lookout, marking the party with a chalk sigil on a crate as they pass
A barrel of 'salted fish' that, when opened, holds smuggled weapons or counterfeit coin
secrets: The conspiracy moves its forged coin and seals through the market hidden in fish barrels, timed to the pre-dawn chaos when the city watch never patrols
One auctioneer's chant is a cipher — the 'prices' he calls are a schedule of shinobi drop-points across the city

keyLocations.name: The Sumō Grounds of Ryūko-en
keyLocations.description: A great circular arena of packed earth and timber tiers, roofed by a suspended canopy hung with four colored tassels for the seasons. At its center sits the dohyō — a raised ring of clay bordered by a buried rope circle, sanctified with salt and sake. Here the realm's mightiest rikishi wrestlers, mountainous men in ceremonial belts, hurl one another to the dirt before roaring crowds while the shōgun's officials watch from cushioned boxes. Champions are demigods of the city, and a wrestler's loyalty — or a fixed bout — can shift the balance of power in Edo. ⚔️
features: The dohyō ring itself: step out of the rope or touch the clay with anything but your feet and you lose
The ritual of salt-throwing and stomping that opens each bout, beloved by the crowd
Private viewing boxes for officials and wealthy patrons, ideal for an overheard conversation
The wrestlers' stable behind the arena, where champions train and gamble and gossip
encounters: A grappling contest in the ring — non-lethal, opposed Athletics, three falls — to win a champion's trust or a wager
A conspirator nobles in a viewing box, overheard if the party can get close without raising suspicion
A champion wrestler, Ōzeki Tetsuwan, who knows a key secret but will only share it with someone who faces him in the ring
secrets: A faction in the conspiracy has been fixing high-stakes bouts to launder counterfeit coin through the betting houses
The champion Tetsuwan despises the fixers and will become a powerful ally if the party wins his respect honestly

keyLocations.name: The Heron's Rest Bathhouse (Sentō)
keyLocations.description: A neighborhood bathhouse of dark cedar and rising steam, marked by a noren curtain dyed with a white heron. Inside, past the shoe-lockers and the attendant's raised platform, lie the washing stations — rows of low stools, wooden buckets, and spigots where every bather scrubs themselves spotless before so much as a toe touches the great shared soaking pools beyond. The water is scalding, the air thick with steam and quiet conversation, and the etiquette is iron: you arrive filthy and leave clean, and you wash before the bath, never in it. It is a place of vulnerability — naked, unarmed, off guard — and therefore a favored place for the city's powerful to speak frankly, and for its assassins to strike.
features: The washing stations: low stools and buckets where one must scrub thoroughly before entering the soaking pool
The great soaking pool, scalding and clouded with steam, where weapons and armor cannot go
The shoe-lockers and clothing baskets at the entrance — where a clever thief or assassin stashes a hidden blade
A back garden with a cold plunge and a rear gate onto an alley, a discreet exit
encounters: A clandestine meeting between two conspirators in the soaking pool, overheard if the party blends in (and observes the etiquette)
An assassin who has hidden a blade in the clothing baskets and waits for the party to disarm and bathe
A friendly elder bather who, charmed, lets slip rumors about who has been meeting whom
secrets: The bathhouse owner launders messages, not money — petitioners leave folded notes in specific shoe-lockers for the conspiracy to collect
A tattooed bather marked with a coiling spider is a sworn agent of the Jorōgumo clan and recognizes others by their ink

keyLocations.name: Karasu-jō, the Crow Castle
keyLocations.description: The shōgun's keep dominates Edo's skyline: a soaring black-walled donjon of five tiered roofs sweeping up like a flight of crows' wings, ringed by white-plastered walls, moats of still green water, and gates within gates. By day it is a fortress of bowing officials and clattering spear-drills; by night it is a maze of lantern-lit corridors, sliding paper screens, and the famous 'nightingale floors' that chirp and sing under any footstep, betraying intruders to the guards. Beneath it all run old stone storm-tunnels and a forgotten shrine-cellar where the conspiracy has made its lair. 🏯
features: The nightingale floors — corridors whose boards chirp under any weight; crossing silently requires Stealth DC 16 or knowledge of the safe path
Sliding paper-screen walls (shōji) that offer concealment but no cover and tear like tissue
The high donjon balconies, reachable across the sweeping rooftops by a daring climber
Hidden storm-tunnels beneath the keep leading to an old shrine-cellar repurposed as a forgery workshop and shinobi nest
encounters: Patrolling castle guards and a captain who must be evaded, bluffed, or fought
A rooftop pursuit by rival shinobi across the donjon's tiered roofs
The climactic confrontation in the shrine-cellar against the conspiracy's leader and her yōkai guardian
secrets: The conspiracy's true aim is not to kill the shōgun but to discredit him — flooding Edo with forged seals so his decrees become worthless and the great clans revolt
The shrine-cellar's old well connects to the fish-market back-channels, explaining how forged coin moves unseen across the whole city

synopsis: Drawn into Edo by a summons from the shōgun's spymaster, the party uncovers a conspiracy of the Jorōgumo shinobi clan — silken assassins who serve a yōkai mistress — flooding the castle town with counterfeit seals and coin to discredit the warlord and topple his rule from within. The investigation winds from the lantern-lit shopping street of Senkō-ji Temple, through a dawn chase across the slick stones of the fish market, into a sumō champion's ring and the steam of a neighborhood bathhouse, gathering allies and cutting through rival shinobi along the way. The trail leads at last beneath the shōgun's own Crow Castle, across singing nightingale floors and sweeping rooftops, to a forgotten shrine-cellar where the spider-clan's mistress and her monstrous guardian wait. The party must expose the forgery, survive the steel of the silent clans, and decide the fate of a city held together by nothing but a warlord's word and a thousand fragile paper lanterns.
hook: A lacquered box, delivered to the party's inn by a child who vanishes before questions can be asked, contains a single black heron feather, a heavy purse of genuine gold, and a folded letter sealed with the crest of Lord Hattori Sōun, the shōgun's spymaster. The letter is terse: counterfeit seals bearing the shōgun's own crest have begun appearing across Edo — on tax writs, on safe-conduct passes, on death warrants. If the forgery is not its rooted out before the Lantern Festival three nights hence, the great clans will lose all faith in the shōgun's authority and the realm will tip into war. Hattori cannot use his own agents; the rot may reach inside his service. He needs outsiders no one in Edo will recognize. Begin at the great red lantern of Senkō-ji at dusk. Tell no one. 🏮

acts.title: Act 1: Beneath the Red Lantern
acts.description: The party arrives in Edo, makes contact with the spymaster's network at the great temple, and begins pulling at the threads of the forgery conspiracy. This act establishes the city, its customs, and its dangers — emphasizing investigation, social maneuvering, and the constant sense of being watched. It culminates in a dawn chase through the fish market and the party's first clash with the silent clans.
objectives: Make contact with the spymaster's courier at Senkō-ji Temple
Uncover the counterfeit seals hidden in the temple's fortune-slip drawers
Learn the forged coin moves through the dawn fish market
Pursue the forger's courier through the market and survive the first shinobi ambush

scenes.name: The Lantern Gate at Dusk
scenes.description: The party arrives at the great vermilion gate of Senkō-ji as the lamps are lit, the giant red lantern glowing like a small sun above the crowd. Their contact is somewhere in the throng of pilgrims and stall-keepers along the covered shopping street — and so, very likely, is someone watching them.
scenes.readAloud: "Dusk settles over Edo in shades of indigo and smoke, and the great vermilion gate of Senkō-ji rises before you, its colossal red lantern aglow from within, painted with a coiling black dragon that seems to writhe as the paper sways. Beyond the gate, a covered street runs arrow-straight toward the temple, lined on both sides with stalls — rice crackers hissing on grills, fans snapping open in a hundred colors, lucky charms swinging on strings. The crowd is a warm river of bodies, the air thick with incense and grilled sweet-bean. Somewhere in all this noise and light, a black heron feather waits for you. And somewhere, perhaps, a pair of eyes that should not be there."

skillChecks.success: Amid the crowd you catch it — a stall-keeper selling fortune charms who wears a single black heron feather tucked into their collar, and who meets your eye for exactly one heartbeat before looking away.
skillChecks.failure: The crowd is a blur of color and motion; your contact, if they are here, has not revealed themselves yet.

skillChecks.success: You notice a second watcher: a lean figure idling too long beneath the eaves across the street, whose gaze tracks you and not the merchandise. You are being followed.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone here seems to be a shopper or a seller; nothing stands out as a threat.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the party's first taste of Edo — lean into sensory detail and the culture. The contact is Kaede, a young woman posing as a charm-seller, sharp-eyed and terse, who works for Hattori. She will not speak openly in the crowd; she palms a folded slip to a party member ('Draw a fortune at the cauldron. The forty-fourth drawer.') and melts away. If players observe bathhouse/temple etiquette and treat locals with respect, they earn goodwill. A pickpocket child may bump them — a test of how they react to the city's poor.
loot: A folded fortune-slip with a hand-inked instruction: 'Cauldron. Drawer 44. Burn this.'
A bundle of incense and a temple luck-charm, pressed on them by a grateful stall-keeper if they were kind (narrative goodwill)

scenes.name: The Forty-Fourth Drawer
scenes.description: Following Kaede's instruction, the party approaches the temple's incense cauldron and the wall of numbered fortune-drawers tended by monks. Drawer forty-four does not hold a paper fortune — it holds proof that the forgery reaches into the temple itself, and the head priest Genshō knows far more than he is willing to say.
scenes.readAloud: "The great bronze cauldron breathes fragrant smoke into the night, and pilgrims crowd close to waft it over their heads for health and fortune. Beside it stands a tall lacquered cabinet of small numbered drawers, where for a coin a monk lets you draw your fate on a slip of paper. You find the forty-fourth drawer. But when you slide it open, there is no fortune inside — only a thin square of folded rice-paper, and pressed into a cake of red wax upon it, the unmistakable crest of the shōgun himself. The wax is still faintly warm. From across the courtyard, a robed priest goes very still, watching you, his knuckles white where he grips his prayer beads."

skillChecks.success: Comparing the wax seal to a genuine writ, you spot the flaw: the crest's central crane has nine tail-feathers instead of eight. This is a forgery — and a superb one, made by a master's hand with access to the true seal's pattern.
skillChecks.failure: The seal looks perfect to you; only a true expert could tell it from the genuine article.

skillChecks.success: Genshō, the head priest, breaks under gentle pressure and a promise of protection. He confesses he was blackmailed — agents threatened his temple, and he was forced to let them use the drawers as a drop-point. He does not know their faces, only that the coin and seals arrive from the river market before dawn.
skillChecks.failure: Genshō stonewalls, terrified, insisting he knows nothing — but his fear itself confirms the temple is compromised.

skillChecks.success: Cornered and frightened, Genshō blurts out a name in panic: 'The Jorōgumo. The spider-weavers. They come from the fish market before the sun. Please — they will kill me for this.'
skillChecks.failure: Genshō faints or flees to the inner sanctuary, and the party loses the chance to question him gently; they'll need another lead.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Genshō is a victim, not a villain — a frightened man trapped between the conspiracy and the shōgun's justice. Play his terror sincerely. Under the loose floor-plank beneath the altar (Investigation DC 16) the party can find a strongbox of forged seals, hard evidence to bring to Hattori. The key clue from this scene: the forged seals and coin enter the city through the dawn fish market. The 'Jorōgumo' name foreshadows the spider-clan and their yōkai mistress.
loot: A genuine letter of safe-conduct from Hattori (lets the party pass city checkpoints and request a single favor from the watch)
A strongbox of forged seals beneath the altar (damning evidence — Investigation DC 16 to find)
Genshō's prayer beads, given in gratitude if the party promises to protect his temple (narrative goodwill)

scenes.name: Dawn at the Fish Market
scenes.description: Before sunrise the party stakes out the roaring fish market, watching for the forgers' delivery. They spot the courier — and when the figure realizes they are made, they bolt, triggering a frantic chase through the slick, crowded aisles that ends in the party's first taste of shinobi steel.
scenes.readAloud: "You reach the riverside while the sky is still the color of a bruise, and the fish market hits you like a wave — torchlight on wet stone, the slap of cleavers through tuna the size of a man, a hundred voices chanting prices in a tongue you cannot follow. Porters sprint past balancing crates; ice-melt and fish-blood make the floor a skating rink. Then you see them: a hooded figure threading the crowd with a sealed fish-barrel cradled too carefully, glancing back once too often. For a single heartbeat your eyes meet across the throng. Then the courier drops the barrel — it bursts, spilling not fish but a glittering tide of silver coin across the stones — and runs."

skillChecks.success: You vault crates and skid through the slick aisles without losing speed, closing the gap on the fleeing courier.
skillChecks.failure: You hit a patch of ice-slick stone and go down hard, taking 1d4 bludgeoning damage and losing ground in the chase.

skillChecks.success: You duck under a hanging net and leap a porter's cart in stride, cutting off the courier's path and forcing them toward a dead-end channel.
skillChecks.failure: You misjudge the leap, crash through a stall, and a furious fishmonger's tumbling crates block your path for a precious moment.

skillChecks.success: You notice the courier is herding you — steering the chase deliberately toward a narrow channel between the boat-docks. It's a trap, and you have a heartbeat to brace for it.
skillChecks.failure: Focused on the runner, you don't see the ambush forming until the dark figures drop from the rooftops.

combatEncounters.tactics: As the chase funnels the party into the cramped boat-channel, three dark-clad shinobi spring the ambush: two drop from the rooftops behind to flank (Spies, using Cunning Action and Sneak Attack), while the Scout looses arrows from a stacked-crate perch before going to melee. They fight to recover or destroy the spilled forged coin, not to the death — at half their number defeated, the survivors throw a smoke-pellet (heavily obscured 10-ft cloud) and attempt to flee across the rooftops. Pre-declared: ambushers have advantage on their first attack against any character who failed the Perception check above.
combatEncounters.terrain: A narrow channel between fish-stalls and boat-docks: slick wet stone (difficult terrain on a failed DC 10 Dex save when dashing), stacked crates and barrels for cover, hanging nets that can be cut to entangle (improvised restrain, DC 12 Str to break free), and dark water on one side — a creature reduced to 0 HP near the edge may topple in.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene shifts the campaign from investigation into action. Let the chase breathe — call for a few honest skill checks with real consequences (a fall, a lost step, a knocked-over stall) before the ambush lands. The shinobi wear no clan marks but one carries a silk cord with a tiny silver spider charm — the Jorōgumo signature. If a shinobi is captured alive, they will say nothing... but the spider charm and a tattoo of a coiling web confirm the clan. The spilled forged coin is more hard evidence. XP: 2 Spies (CR 1, 200 each) + 1 Scout (CR 1/2, 100) = 500 XP total, divided among the party.
loot: A silk cord with a silver spider charm (Jorōgumo clan token — evidence and a recognition-sign the party can later use to bluff)
Roughly 40 gp in genuine coin spilled and recoverable from the burst barrel (the rest is forged and worthless)
A captured shinobi's set of climbing claws (tekagi) — advantage on Athletics checks to climb sheer walls (1 set)

acts.title: Act 2: The Floating World
acts.description: Armed with the Jorōgumo name, the party works the city's underbelly to find the spider-clan's foothold inside the castle. This act sprawls across Edo's most vivid settings — the sumō arena, the bathhouse, the lantern districts — blending social intrigue, an honest contest of strength, and a deadly trap. It builds toward the discovery that the conspiracy operates from beneath the shōgun's own keep, and ends with a brutal fight against a yōkai guardian.
objectives: Win the trust of the sumō champion Tetsuwan and expose the fixed bouts
Survive the bathhouse trap and identify the Jorōgumo agent
Discover how the conspiracy reaches inside the Crow Castle
Defeat the jorōgumo spider-yōkai guarding the river entrance

scenes.name: The Champion's Ring
scenes.description: The trail of fixed bets leads to the great sumō arena, where the champion Ōzeki Tetsuwan holds court. He knows who has been laundering coin through the betting houses — but he is a man of old honor and will not whisper secrets to strangers. He'll talk only to someone who steps onto the clay and faces him fairly.
scenes.readAloud: "The sumō grounds thunder with the stamping of ten thousand feet. Beneath a hanging canopy bright with seasonal tassels, two mountains of men circle the raised clay ring, fling salt skyward in glittering arcs, and crash together like landslides while the crowd bays. When the bout ends, the victor turns toward you — Ōzeki Tetsuwan, the realm's grand champion, a man built like a temple bell, his small eyes shrewd in a broad calm face. He has been watching you watch him. 'You ask many questions about my sport,' he rumbles, beckoning you toward the ring with one massive hand. 'Words are cheap in the Floating World. The dohyō does not lie. Stand on the clay with me, and we will see what kind of person asks such questions.'"

skillChecks.success: You hold your footing against the champion's charge and even force him a step back; the crowd gasps. Win or lose the bout, your honest effort earns Tetsuwan's deep respect.
skillChecks.failure: Tetsuwan plants you in the clay with terrifying ease — but you rose, you bowed, and you did not whine. He respects that more than a cheap victory.

skillChecks.success: Watching the betting boxes during the bouts, you spot it: a cluster of nobles whose wagers always 'lose' by exactly the same suspicious margins, the coin vanishing into a back room. The bouts are being fixed to launder money.
skillChecks.failure: The betting is a frenzy of coin and shouting; you can't untangle the legitimate wagers from the crooked ones without a guide.

skillChecks.success: Having met him with honor in the ring, you find Tetsuwan an open ally. He names the fixers — agents who pay in coin stamped with a tiny spider — and tells you their go-between bathes nightly at the Heron's Rest. He offers his fame and fists if you need them.
skillChecks.failure: Tetsuwan likes you but stays cautious; he'll point you to the bathhouse lead but won't yet put his own neck on the block.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The sumō bout is a non-lethal contest of honor — run it as a best-of-three opposed Athletics (or Athletics vs. the champion's +6), but the OUTCOME of winning or losing matters far less than HOW the player conducts themselves. Tetsuwan values courage, honesty, and grace in defeat over victory. This is a culture beat: respect the ring's rituals (salt, the bow) and he opens up. He becomes a recurring ally who can be called on in Act 3 to create a diversion or stand at the party's side. Key intel: the Jorōgumo go-between can be found at the Heron's Rest bathhouse after dark.
loot: A champion's ceremonial salt-pouch from Tetsuwan, a token of friendship (present it to any sumō stable or sporting house for a warm welcome and free lodging)
A list of the fixed-bout nobles, several of whom hold offices inside the Crow Castle (a thread leading to Act 3)

scenes.name: Steam and Steel
scenes.description: At the Heron's Rest bathhouse the party must identify the Jorōgumo go-between among the bathers — which means disarming, undressing, and observing the strict etiquette of the bath. It is the most vulnerable they will ever be, and the spider-clan knows it. An assassin has hidden a blade among the clothing baskets and waits for them to lower their guard.
scenes.readAloud: "The noren curtain with its white heron parts onto warmth and the smell of cedar. An attendant nods you toward the lockers — shoes off, clothes folded into baskets, weapons left behind, for no steel touches the bath. Beyond, rows of low stools and wooden buckets line the washing wall, where every bather scours themselves spotless before the soaking pool: here, you arrive filthy and you leave clean, and you never, ever bring soap or grime into the shared water. Through the rising steam you can just make out figures reclining in the great clouded pool, their voices low and frank, their guards entirely down. Somewhere among them is the person you seek. And somewhere, perhaps, someone who seeks you."

skillChecks.success: Through the steam you mark your quarry: a lean bather whose shoulder bears a tattoo of a coiling spider's web, speaking in hushed tones to a castle official about 'the festival night' and 'the well below.' This is the Jorōgumo go-between.
skillChecks.failure: The steam and the dim light make every bather a vague shape; you cannot pick out your target without getting closer and risking notice.

skillChecks.success: As you fold your clothes, you notice one of the wicker baskets sits slightly askew — and beneath a stranger's robe, the unmistakable glint of an oiled blade. The bath is a trap. You have a heartbeat to act before it springs.
skillChecks.failure: You disarm and bathe like everyone else, never seeing the hidden weapon — the assassin gets the drop on you (they act first and with advantage when the trap springs).

skillChecks.success: Showing the silver spider charm taken in the market, you pass yourself off as a fellow clan agent long enough to draw the go-between into revealing the plan: the forgers work from a shrine-cellar beneath the castle, reached by an old well from the river.
skillChecks.failure: Your bluff rings false; the go-between's eyes narrow, and the trap springs early.

combatEncounters.tactics: When the trap springs, the Assassin strikes from concealment with the hidden blade — pre-declared: if the party failed the Perception check above, the Assassin acts in a surprise round and lands its Assassinate critical on its first hit. The two Spies, soaking innocently moments before, draw hidden daggers and flank. The party is unarmored and likely separated from their weapons (improvised unarmed/grapple options, or a desperate Athletics DC 12 dash to the lockers to recover a weapon, costing their action). The scalding pool and slick tile are hazards: shoving a foe into the soaking pool deals 1d6 fire (scald) damage and imposes disadvantage on their next attack. The Assassin fights to kill the witnesses, then flee; the Spies cover the retreat.
combatEncounters.terrain: Steam-filled bathhouse (lightly obscured throughout — disadvantage on Perception sight checks). Wet tile floor (DC 10 Dex save when Dashing or fall prone). The scalding soaking pool (entering or being shoved in: 1d6 fire damage). Clothing lockers 20 ft away hold the party's confiscated weapons and armor. Flimsy wooden screens provide concealment but no cover.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the campaign's tension-peak trap: the party fights at their most vulnerable, unarmed and unarmored. Reward players who clocked the etiquette and the askew basket. The culture beat is real and useful — players who scrub properly at the wash-stations and keep their towel out of the water blend in perfectly; players who blunder in dirty draw every eye and lose any chance of surprise. Whether by interrogation, the Deception bluff, or recovering it from a fallen agent, the party must leave with the crucial intel: the conspiracy operates from a shrine-cellar beneath the Crow Castle, reached via an old well connected to the river. XP: 1 Assassin (CR 8, 3900) is steep for this level — scale to 1 Assassin run cautiously OR substitute a Scout-statted blade-master (CR 1/2, 100) plus 2 Spies (200 each) for a fairer 500 XP. Use the Assassin only for a deadly, high-Difficulty table; honor the lethality if you do.
loot: The go-between's lacquered message-case, holding a map of the castle's storm-tunnels and a forged festival-night safe-conduct (lets the party enter the castle grounds)
A vial of black lotus paste (poison, applies 1d6 poison damage to a weapon for one hit; 3 doses) recovered from the Assassin
Roughly 60 gp in genuine coin and a pair of fine silk under-robes worth 25 gp

scenes.name: The Well Below the Crow
scenes.description: Following the map, the party descends through the river's back-channels into the old storm-tunnels beneath the Crow Castle, toward the shrine-cellar lair. But the spider-clan does not leave its threshold unguarded — a true yōkai, a jorōgumo spider-demon in the shape of a beautiful woman above and a monstrous spider below, has woven the flooded tunnel into her web.
scenes.readAloud: "The old well swallows you into wet darkness, and you wade through storm-tunnels that stink of brine and rot, the castle's foundations groaning overhead. The map leads you toward a flickering light — and then your torch catches the webs. They sheet the entire tunnel ahead, thick as ship's rigging, beaded with water and wrapped, here and there, around the husks of those who came before. At the center of the web, something stirs and unfolds. From the waist up she is a woman of terrible beauty, pale and smiling, her black hair hanging like silk. From the waist down she is a spider the size of a horse, eight glistening legs ticking against the stone. 'Little flies,' she croons, and her voice is a lullaby. 'You buzzed so loudly. I have been so hungry.' 🕷️"

skillChecks.success: You recognize the creature: a jorōgumo, a spider-yōkai that beguiles prey with illusion and song before binding it in web. Her beguiling voice can charm — covering your ears or fixing your gaze on her lower half, not her face, grants advantage to resist.
skillChecks.failure: You know only that this is a monster of the old tales come horribly real, and that her voice makes your thoughts go soft.

skillChecks.success: You read the web's architecture and find the tunnel's dry edges and load-bearing strands — safe footing that avoids the worst entangling sheets and even a strand that, if cut, drops a curtain of web on the yōkai herself.
skillChecks.failure: The webbing is a featureless maze; moving through it is treacherous (web is difficult terrain and may restrain the careless).

enemies: 1 Jorōgumo (use Drider stats, CR 6, reflavored as a spider-yōkai)
combatEncounters.tactics: The jorōgumo opens by trying to charm with her song (treat as the Drider's spellcasting / a Charm effect, Wis save DC 14; advantage to resist for any character not looking at her face, per the Arcana check). She loves her web: the tunnel is difficult terrain, and her Web attack restrains (DC 13 Str/Dex to escape, AC 10 to burn or cut the strand). She stays in the webbed center where her brood funnels prey to her, raking with her bite and longsword while the two Giant Spiders web and flank from the ceiling. Pre-declared: she fights to the death — this is her threshold and her larder, and she will not yield it. Reducing the brood frees the party to focus her down.
combatEncounters.terrain: A flooded storm-tunnel choked with webbing: web-sheets are difficult terrain and can restrain (escape DC 13); knee-deep brackish water in the low channel (difficult terrain, douses fire-strands); a few dry stone ledges for safe footing (per Survival check). A cut load-bearing strand can drop a web-curtain on a 10-ft area (Dex save DC 13 or restrained). Open flame versus the dry webbing spreads fire — dramatic, but risks the whole tunnel.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the Act 2 boss and the campaign's monster set-piece — play the jorōgumo as seductive, ancient, and utterly without mercy, a beauty-and-horror yōkai straight from folklore. Her charm-song is the real danger; telegraph the 'don't look at her face' counter through the Arcana check so clever players feel rewarded. Honor the dice: if a charmed character walks into her web, that's a real consequence. Beyond her lies the shrine-cellar and the climb to the conspiracy's leader. XP: Drider (CR 6, 2300) + 2 Giant Spiders (CR 1, 200 each) = 2700 XP total, divided among the party — a hefty, well-earned haul. Fire vs. web is a legitimate tactic; reward it, but make the spreading flames a complication that threatens everyone.
loot: A great pearl of compressed spider-silk (worth 200 gp, sells to any silk merchant or yōkai-scholar)
Cocooned among her victims: a castle guard's uniform and signet (a perfect disguise for entering the keep above)
Strands of jorōgumo silk that can be woven into a single Cloak of Spider-Silk (advantage on Stealth checks made to hide; 1 such cloak's worth of material)
A waterlogged ledger in her lair detailing every forged-seal shipment — the smoking-gun evidence Hattori needs

acts.title: Act 3: The Crow's Shadow
acts.description: The party ascends into the shōgun's own Crow Castle on the night of the Lantern Festival to expose and stop the conspiracy at its source. This act is the action-thriller climax: a tense infiltration across singing nightingale floors, a breathless rooftop pursuit by rival shinobi, and a final confrontation with the spider-clan's mistress and her oni enforcer in the shrine-cellar below. The party's choices decide the fate of the warlord's rule and the city's fragile peace.
objectives: Infiltrate the Crow Castle on Lantern Festival night
Cross the nightingale floors and evade or defeat the castle guard
Survive the rooftop pursuit by the Jorōgumo clan
Confront the conspiracy's mistress and her oni enforcer in the shrine-cellar
Decide the fate of the conspiracy and the evidence — and what the shōgun will be told

scenes.name: The Nightingale Floors
scenes.description: Disguised and slipping through the Lantern Festival crowds, the party penetrates the Crow Castle's inner keep — and meets its famous defense: the nightingale floors, corridors of cunning boards that chirp like songbirds under any footstep, betraying intruders to the patrolling guard.
scenes.readAloud: "Above you the great black donjon blazes with festival lanterns, five tiers of sweeping crow-wing roofs against a sky bursting with fireworks. Inside, past the bowing officials and the spear-racks, the noise falls away. A long corridor of pale polished wood stretches before you, lined with sliding paper screens, lit by paper lamps that throw soft amber light. You take one step — and the floor sings. A bright, sweet chirp, like a nightingale, rises from beneath your foot and echoes down the hall. These are the keep's famous singing floors, laid so that no foot can fall without raising an alarm. Somewhere ahead, a guard's voice calls a question into the dark."

skillChecks.success: You find the rhythm of the safe boards — heel light, weight forward, hugging the wall where the nails bite deepest — and ghost down the singing corridor in near silence, the floor barely whispering beneath you.
skillChecks.failure: The floor erupts in song with every step. A patrol rounds the corner; you must hide, bluff, or fight (proceed to the guard encounter).

skillChecks.success: In the stolen castle uniform and signet, you wave off the responding guards with a curt festival-night excuse, and they bow and withdraw. You're in.
skillChecks.failure: Your story doesn't hold under the guard captain's scrutiny; he calls for the corridor to be sealed (proceed to the guard encounter).

skillChecks.success: You spot the trick of the floor: a single line of darker, older boards along the western wall runs silent — the path the castle's own spies use. Following it lets the whole party cross without a sound.
skillChecks.failure: Every board looks identical; there is no shortcut but skill and nerve.

combatEncounters.tactics: Triggered only if the party sets off the floors and fails to bluff. The Veteran captain bellows for reinforcements (a turn-three timer: if the fight isn't ended or the party fled within three rounds, a second patrol arrives) while the four Guards form a spear-wall across the narrow corridor — they fight defensively, aiming to delay and contain rather than kill, since they believe they face mere intruders, not assassins. The paper screens tear like tissue (no cover, but an escape route to the rooftops). Pre-declared: the party can flee onto the roofs at any point, transitioning directly to the next scene's pursuit.
combatEncounters.terrain: A narrow keep corridor (10 ft wide): nightingale floors (any Dash or careless movement is loud — irrelevant once combat is joined, but the noise summons the timer-reinforcements). Sliding paper screens (shōji) line both walls — they grant total concealment for one moment but no cover, and bursting through one opens onto a balcony and the rooftop route. Paper lamps can be knocked down to start a small, spreading fire (a hazard and a distraction).

scenes.roleplayNotes: Reward a quiet approach lavishly — a party that crosses by Stealth, Deception, or the spies' path skips the fight entirely and reaches the climax fresh. The guards are honest soldiers doing their duty, not villains; a captured guard can be reasoned with or spared, and killing the shōgun's own men has consequences for how the finale lands. This is the calm-before-the-storm beat: tense, quiet, every footstep a gamble. If the alarm goes up, transition smoothly into the rooftop chase. XP only if combat occurs: 4 Guards (CR 1/8, 25 each = 100) + 1 Veteran (CR 3, 700) = 800 XP, divided among the party.
loot: A master-key ring to the keep's inner doors (taken from the captain or found on the spies' path)
The guard captain's whistle (blow it to summon — or misdirect — a patrol, once)

scenes.name: Across the Crow's Wings
scenes.description: Whether fleeing the alarm or racing the clock to reach the shrine-cellar's upper entrance, the party takes to the castle's sweeping tiered rooftops under exploding fireworks — and the Jorōgumo clan, realizing their plot is unraveling, send their rooftop runners to cut the party down before they can reach the mistress below.
scenes.readAloud: "You burst onto the rooftops and the festival sky swallows you — fireworks blooming red and gold, the tiered roofs of the great donjon sweeping away below like the wings of a diving crow, slick black tiles falling steeply to lantern-lit courtyards a hundred feet down. The wind tears at your clothes. And then you see them: dark shapes detaching from the shadows of the gables, running the ridgelines toward you with silent, terrible speed, blades drawn, silver spider-charms glinting at their throats. The Jorōgumo have come to finish this on the roof of the warlord's own house. 🌃⚔️"

skillChecks.success: You run the steep tiles like flat ground, leaping the gaps between roofs and keeping your feet where others would fall screaming into the dark.
skillChecks.failure: A tile cracks loose underfoot; you slide toward the edge and must make a DC 14 Dexterity save or fall — catching a gutter for 1d6 damage, or plunging if you fail that too.

skillChecks.success: You make the long leap to the next tier of roof and haul a struggling ally up after you, keeping the party together across the gap.
skillChecks.failure: You make the jump but land hard and winded, losing your footing's momentum (start your next turn at half movement).

skillChecks.success: You spot the ambusher's favorite trick before it lands — a near-invisible trip-cord of spider-silk strung across the ridgeline — and warn the party in time to leap or cut it.
skillChecks.failure: Someone hits the trip-cord at a dead run; that character makes a DC 14 Dex save or is sent sprawling toward the roof's edge.

enemies: 1 Assassin OR Scout (clan blade-master — see note)
combatEncounters.tactics: A running fight across the tiered roofs. The Spies use Cunning Action to dash and disengage along the ridgelines, striking with Sneak Attack and retreating, trying to bleed the party while the steep tiles and gaps do half the work. The blade-master harries whoever leads, aiming to isolate and drop a single character over the edge. Pre-declared environmental rule: any creature reduced to 0 HP, or that fails a save while within 5 ft of a roof-edge, falls — 2d6 to 6d6 bludgeoning depending on the tier (telegraph the height before any roll). The Jorōgumo fight to stop the party reaching the cellar, not to win outright; if three or more fall, the rest break off into the night. Fireworks periodically flash the rooftops in bright light (a charmed or hidden creature is briefly revealed).
combatEncounters.terrain: Steep tiered roofs of slick black tile (difficult terrain; any Dash requires a DC 13 Acrobatics check or the character slides 10 ft toward the nearest edge). Gaps of 5–15 ft between roof-tiers (cleared by Athletics/Acrobatics, DC scaling with distance). Roof-ridges are narrow (5 ft — a creature shoved or knocked prone here risks a fall). The deadly fall is the real second enemy: use it honestly and telegraph it every time.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the cinematic action high-point — keep it fast, vertical, and dangerous, with fireworks strobing the sky. The fall is the star of the scene: declare the height and the damage BEFORE any edge-roll, and honor the result. A shoved enemy goes over; so does a careless hero. Use the blade-master (Assassin for a deadly table, Scout for a fair one) sparingly and tactically. This scene can be skipped or shortened if the party reached the roofs by stealth without raising the alarm — in that case, run a single tense ambush by 2 Spies instead. XP (full version): 3 Spies (CR 1, 200 each = 600) + 1 Scout (CR 1/2, 100) = 700 XP, or +3800 if you used the Assassin (CR 8) for a deadly table. Divide among the party.
loot: A grappling-hook and silk line (kaginawa) — advantage on Athletics checks to climb or swing, 1 set
A Jorōgumo runner's mask and dark garb (a complete shinobi disguise, 1 set)
A scorched festival lantern that, by chance, lit the party's victory in gold (narrative trophy)

scenes.name: The Spider in the Shrine
scenes.description: Below the singing floors and the festival roofs, in a forgotten shrine-cellar where the conspiracy was woven, the party finally faces its architect: Lady Kumohime, mistress of the Jorōgumo clan, surrounded by her forgery-presses and forged seals — and guarded by a towering oni, a horned demon-ogre sworn to her service. Here the plot, the city's fate, and the party's resolve all come to a head.
scenes.readAloud: "A narrow stair winds down beneath the keep into an old shrine-cellar, its forgotten altar long since shoved aside to make room for the machinery of treason: forgery-presses, racks of carved seal-stamps, baskets heaped with rice-paper and red wax, all lit by the cold blue glow of paper lanterns. At the center of it stands a woman in a twelve-layered robe of midnight silk, beautiful and composed, a single black heron feather in her piled black hair — Lady Kumohime, mistress of the spider-clan. She does not flee, does not flinch. She only smiles, and lays down the seal she was inspecting. 'So,' she says softly, 'the warlord found himself some flies after all.' Behind her, a shape unfolds from the shadows — nine feet of corded red muscle, a single horn jutting from its brow, an iron club big as a man across its shoulder. The oni's eyes find you, and it grins. 'Then let them be eaten.' 👹"

skillChecks.success: You find the crack in Kumohime's composure — her contempt for the shōgun masks an old, genuine grievance — and offer her a path that isn't death: surrender the evidence and the clan's lives for her testimony. She hesitates. The oni does not have to fight, if she calls it off.
skillChecks.failure: Kumohime laughs at your words; she has staked everything on this night and will not be talked out of it. The oni attacks.

skillChecks.success: You read the truth beneath her calm: Kumohime never meant to kill the shōgun — she means to make his word worthless, to drown his authority in forged seals so the great clans rise against him. Knowing the true plot lets you speak to her real aim (advantage on the Persuasion attempt above).
skillChecks.failure: Her motives stay veiled behind that serene smile; she is simply, to all appearances, a traitor and an assassin.

skillChecks.success: You recall the oni's weaknesses from the old tales: it can turn invisible and change shape, and it loathes the scattering of blessed soybeans and the smell of sardine and holly — small ritual wards that can break its nerve or banish its illusions for a round.
skillChecks.failure: You know only that an oni is a thing of terrible strength and dark magic, to be fought with steel and prayer.

enemies: Lady Kumohime (use Mage or Spy stats — see note)
combatEncounters.tactics: The Oni is the muscle: it opens with its Change Shape or Invisibility to gain the jump, then wades in with its greatclub (Multiattack, reach) and its frightening Regeneration, targeting spellcasters first. Kumohime hangs back among the presses, casting (or throwing poisoned needles, if using Spy stats) and using the cluttered cellar for cover, directing the oni and trying to destroy the ledger-evidence in the flames of a knocked-over lantern. Pre-declared, honor it: the Oni fights to the death and its Regeneration (10 HP/turn unless it took fire or acid damage that turn) means the party should be steered toward the braziers and lanterns — fire shuts the healing off. If the Persuasion path succeeded, Kumohime calls the oni off and surrenders, and there is no fight. If reduced to 0 HP without fire that turn, the Oni keeps regenerating — make the fire matter. A loose lantern can ignite the paper-stacked cellar (spreading hazard: 1d6 fire to anyone in a growing burning zone each round) — dramatic, dangerous, and a real way to deny the oni its healing.
combatEncounters.terrain: A cramped, cluttered shrine-cellar: forgery-presses and seal-racks (cover, and improvised weapons/obstacles), baskets of paper and wax (extremely flammable — fire spreads to a new 10-ft zone each round once started), blue paper lanterns hanging low (knock one down to ignite the room), the old shrine-altar shoved to one wall (anyone praying at it for inspiration may grant an ally advantage, DM's discretion), and a single narrow stair as the only exit (a bottleneck for a fleeing — or trapped — combatant).

scenes.roleplayNotes: The campaign's climax, and a genuine choice. Kumohime is a true believer, not a cackling villain — she sees the shōgun as a tyrant and her forgery-war as a bloodless revolution. The high-DC Persuasion path (informed by the Insight read of her real plot) lets a clever, silver-tongued party end the conspiracy WITHOUT the oni fight, taking her alive for Hattori's justice — a valid and rewarding outcome. If steel is drawn, run the oni honestly: its Regeneration is the puzzle, and fire is the answer the Arcana/terrain clues point toward — never fudge its HP, make the players solve it. For Kumohime's own stats, use Mage (CR 6) for a spellcasting duel or Spy (CR 1) with poisoned needles for a lighter touch; choose to fit your table's level and the oni's weight. Honor a TPK if the dice and fire turn against the party — but the Persuasion door means death is never the only path. XP: Oni (CR 7, 2900) + Kumohime as Mage (CR 6, 2300) = 5200 XP, or +200 if using Spy stats; award the Persuasion-resolution path EQUAL milestone XP (treat as 5200) — talking down the villain is worth as much as killing her. Divide among the party.
loot: Lady Kumohime's twelve-layered silk robe and heron-feather hairpin (worth 250 gp; the hairpin is a recognized clan-relic)
The Oni's iron greatclub (a Maul; if claimed and re-forged, a master smith can make it a +1 Maul for a price)
The conspiracy's master seal-die — the carved master-stamp used to forge the shōgun's crest (the single most important piece of evidence; whoever holds it controls the forgery)
A war-chest of 300 gp in genuine coin meant to pay the clan, plus the complete forgery-ledger naming every corrupt official

scenes.name: The Word of the Shōgun
scenes.description: With the conspiracy broken, the party carries the evidence — the master seal-die, the ledger, the captives — back into the lantern-lit city to Hattori the spymaster, and through him to the shōgun himself. What they reveal, what they conceal, and whom they spare will shape Edo for a generation.
scenes.readAloud: "You climb out of the dark beneath the castle into a city still ablaze with the Lantern Festival — ten thousand paper lights drifting down the canals, fireworks fading to smoke, the crowds laughing, blissfully unaware of how close their world came to unraveling tonight. Lord Hattori Sōun waits for you on a quiet bridge, the black heron of his crest dark against the lamplight, his face unreadable. 'You have the evidence,' he says. It is not quite a question. In your hands you hold the master seal-die that forged a warlord's name, a ledger that could end a dozen careers, and the fate of more than one life that hangs on your next words. Behind Hattori, far across the water, the great donjon of the Crow Castle stands black and serene against the festival sky, the shōgun within none the wiser — for now."

skillChecks.success: You convince Hattori to be merciful where mercy is earned — sparing the blackmailed priest Genshō, the coerced officials, even Kumohime if she surrendered to testify. Your judgment earns the spymaster's lasting trust and the party a standing place in the shōgun's favor.
skillChecks.failure: Hattori takes the evidence and metes out a harsher justice than you'd have chosen; the conspiracy is crushed, but some who deserved mercy are swept up with the guilty.

skillChecks.success: You read Hattori truly: he is loyal, but ambitious, and he is weighing whether the master seal-die is too dangerous to hand to the shōgun — or too useful to give up. Knowing this, you can guide where that terrible little object ends up.
skillChecks.failure: Hattori's intentions stay locked behind his courtier's calm; you hand over the evidence and trust to his honor.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The denouement and the moral weight of the campaign. The master seal-die is the dramatic crux: destroyed, it ends the threat forever; surrendered to the shōgun, it restores his authority; kept by Hattori — or the party — it is a weapon that could forge the warlord's word at will. Let the players decide. Their choices about mercy (Genshō, the coerced officials, a surrendered Kumohime) and about the seal-die determine Edo's future and Hattori's regard. Reward integrity. If they hand over everything and counsel mercy, the shōgun's quiet gratitude opens doors across the realm for future adventures. There is no single right answer — only the kind of heroes the players chose to be in the Floating World. 🏮
loot: Hattori's reward: 500 gp and a black heron token granting the party safe passage and a standing favor anywhere the shōgun's writ runs
If the party counseled mercy and protected Genshō: the temple of Senkō-ji grants them a permanent blessing-charm and free sanctuary
If the party won Tetsuwan's friendship in Act 2: the champion gifts each of them a ceremonial belt-cord, marking them as honored guests of every sumō stable in Edo

culturalCodex.topic: Sensō-ji Temple & Nakamise-dōri (the Lantern Gate and shopping street)
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Sensō-ji in Asakusa, Tokyo is the city's oldest temple. Its outer Kaminari-mon ('Thunder Gate') hangs a giant red paper lantern, and the Nakamise-dōri shopping street leading to the temple is lined with stalls selling snacks and souvenirs. It's free to enter, open daily, and easily reached via Asakusa Station. Draw an o-mikuji fortune slip for 100 yen; if it's bad luck, tie it to the rack and leave it behind.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In this adventure, 'Senkō-ji' hides forged shōgunate seals in its fortune-slip drawers and a blackmailed priest passing messages for a spider-clan. The real Sensō-ji is a peaceful, bustling temple — there are no shinobi in the incense smoke.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Sumō is Japan's national sport. Wrestlers (rikishi) fight in a clay ring called the dohyō; you win by forcing your opponent out of the ring or making any part of their body other than the soles of their feet touch the ground. Bouts are very short — often seconds — and preceded by ritual salt-throwing and stomping. You can watch a real tournament (basho) in Tokyo at the Ryōgoku Kokugikan arena (tournaments run several times a year), or watch morning practice at a sumō stable.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The campaign's champion 'Tetsuwan' and the fixed-bout money-laundering plot are invented. Real sumō is fiercely traditional and the bouts are honest sport, not a cover for criminal conspiracies.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: At a Japanese public bath (sentō) or hot spring (onsen) you wash THOROUGHLY at the washing stations BEFORE entering the shared soaking pool — soap and shampoo never go in the bath water. You bathe naked; swimsuits aren't worn. The small towel never touches the bath water (people fold it and rest it on their head or set it aside). Tie up long hair. Many baths restrict or forbid visible tattoos, though some are tattoo-friendly or offer cover stickers — check ahead. Baths are usually separated by gender.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The 'Heron's Rest' bathhouse hides assassins' blades in the clothing baskets and is a drop-point for secret messages. A real sentō is just a clean, relaxing, slightly steamy place to soak — the only danger is forgetting to wash first.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Modern Tokyo's convenience stores (konbini) — 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Lawson — are genuinely excellent and everywhere. They have surprisingly good, cheap fresh food (onigiri rice balls, sandwiches, hot meals), clean restrooms, ATMs that take foreign cards (7-Eleven's are the most reliable), and you can pay bills, buy event tickets, and ship luggage. They're open 24/7 and a lifeline for any traveler.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: There are obviously no konbini in a mythic feudal Edo — the closest equivalent in-world is the Nakamise-style stall street or the fish market. This entry is purely a real-Tokyo travel tip.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Japan does not have a tipping culture, and leaving a tip can actually cause confusion or mild offense — good service is simply expected and included. Don't tip in restaurants, taxis, or hotels. If you ever do need to hand over money (paying a bill), it often goes onto a small tray (the register tray) rather than directly into someone's hand. Just say 'gochisōsama deshita' ('thank you for the meal') and you're golden.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the Floating World of the adventure, coin changes hands constantly — bribes, wagers, and forged silver. That's drama. In real modern Japan, keep your tip in your pocket.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: A few words go a long way. 'Eki' (駅) = train station — so 'Tokyo-eki' is Tokyo Station. 'Ikura desu ka?' = 'How much is it?' 'Toire wa doko desu ka?' = 'Where is the toilet?' Also handy: 'Sumimasen' (excuse me / sorry / thank-you-for-trouble — the swiss-army-knife word), 'Arigatō gozaimasu' (thank you), and 'Eigo ga hanasemasu ka?' ('Do you speak English?'). A small bow with any of these earns a lot of warmth.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: NPCs in the campaign speak in stylized 'mythic' cadence for flavor. The phrases above are the real, practical ones that will actually help you navigate Tokyo today.

culturalCodex.topic: The dawn fish market (Toyosu / former Tsukiji)
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Tokyo's famous tuna auctions moved in 2018 from the old Tsukiji market to the modern Toyosu Market, where you can watch the pre-dawn tuna auction from observation decks (registration may be required for the closest viewing). The neighboring Tsukiji Outer Market still thrives with food stalls and fresh sushi breakfasts. Go early — the action is at dawn — and remember it's a working market, so stay out of the porters' way.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The adventure's 'Uogashi' market hides smuggled forged coin in fish barrels and hosts a rooftop shinobi ambush. The real market hides nothing more sinister than extremely fresh tuna and very busy forklifts.

npcsInvolved.name: Lord Hattori Sōun
npcsInvolved.description: The shōgun's spymaster, a lean, soft-spoken man of middle years whose plain dark robes and unhurried courtesy conceal one of the sharpest minds in Edo. He wears the crest of a black heron and is never quite where you expect him to be. He trusts almost no one — which is exactly why he hired outsiders.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Hattori serves the shōgun's authority above all, and he knows the forgery plot could topple the realm into civil war. Unable to trust his own compromised service, he recruits the party as deniable, unknown agents. Loyal but quietly ambitious, he must himself decide what to do with the dangerous master seal-die once it's recovered.

npcsInvolved.name: Kaede
npcsInvolved.description: A sharp-eyed young woman who works Hattori's network under the cover of a temple charm-seller, marked by a single black heron feather. Terse, quick, and brave, she moves through Edo's crowds like water and knows every back-alley and rooftop in the Asakura district.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Loyal to Hattori and to the city's fragile peace, Kaede risks her life passing messages and shadowing suspects. She can become a recurring guide and ally, feeding the party leads and watching their backs — if they prove worthy of trust.

npcsInvolved.name: Priest Genshō
npcsInvolved.description: The aging head priest of Senkō-ji temple, a gentle, frightened man whose temple was turned into a drop-point for forged seals under threat. He grips his prayer beads white-knuckled and is desperate to protect his monks and his sanctuary from the spider-clan's reach.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Genshō never wanted any part of treason; he was blackmailed and terrified into compliance. He longs only to free his temple from the conspiracy's grip. Treated with compassion, he becomes a grateful informant; the party's choice to protect or expose him is one of the campaign's moral beats.

npcsInvolved.name: Ōzeki Tetsuwan
npcsInvolved.description: The realm's grand sumō champion, a man built like a temple bell with a broad, calm face and shrewd eyes that miss nothing. A traditionalist of deep personal honor, he despises the fixers corrupting his beloved sport and judges people not by their words but by how they conduct themselves in the ring.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Tetsuwan wants the betting-house corruption purged from sumō and will ally with anyone who meets him honestly on the clay. Won over, he lends his fame, his fists, and the loyalty of every sumō stable in Edo — a powerful friend for the climax and beyond.

npcsInvolved.name: The Jorōgumo (Spider-Yōkai)
npcsInvolved.description: An ancient spider-demon dwelling in the flooded tunnels beneath the Crow Castle — a woman of terrible beauty from the waist up, a horse-sized spider below, who beguiles prey with an illusory lullaby before binding them in her web. She is the clan's threshold-guardian and its monstrous patron.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Pure, patient hunger. She guards the conspiracy's river-entrance not from loyalty but because the steady stream of intruders feeds her. She cannot be reasoned with, only resisted and slain — her charm-song is the deadliest thing about her.

npcsInvolved.name: Lady Kumohime
npcsInvolved.description: The serene, formidable mistress of the Jorōgumo shinobi clan, who appears in a twelve-layered robe of midnight silk with a single black heron feather in her hair. Composed, intelligent, and utterly unafraid, she is the architect of the entire forgery-war — and a true believer, not a cackling villain.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Kumohime sees the shōgun as a tyrant and means to topple him not with an assassin's blade but by drowning his authority in forged seals until his word is worthless and the great clans revolt. She has staked her clan's survival on this gambit. She can be fought to the death — or, by a party that grasps her real grievance, talked into surrendering for justice and testimony.

rewards.xp: Approximately 10,000–14,000 XP across the campaign (the Persuasion-resolution of the finale awards equal milestone XP to the combat path) — enough to carry a party of four from level 5 toward level 7. Award XP per the post-encounter checklist after every encounter and milestone.
rewards.gold: Roughly 800+ gp total (40 gp market coin, ~60 gp bathhouse, 200 gp silk pearl, 300 gp clan war-chest, 250 gp Kumohime's robe/hairpin, 500 gp Hattori's reward — less any forged, worthless coin)
items: The Master Seal-Die (campaign-defining plot item — the carved stamp that forged the shōgun's crest; its fate is the players' choice)
Cloak of Spider-Silk (advantage on Stealth checks to hide)
The Oni's iron greatclub (a Maul; can be re-forged into a +1 Maul by a master smith)
Climbing claws (tekagi), grappling-hook and silk line (kaginawa) — shinobi gear granting advantage on climbing/swinging
Black lotus paste (weapon poison, 3 doses) and the complete forgery-ledger naming every corrupt official
Hattori's black heron token (safe passage and a standing favor anywhere the shōgun's writ runs)
rewards.story: The party has unmasked and broken a conspiracy that would have toppled the shōgun's rule and plunged the realm into civil war. Their choices — what to reveal, whom to spare, and where the dangerous master seal-die ends up — shape Edo for a generation. Mercy earns the gratitude of priests, champions, and the spymaster himself; ruthlessness crushes the plot but leaves scars. Word of outsiders who saved the Floating World from the shadows will open doors — and attract dangers — across the whole realm, setting the stage for adventures to come. 🏯

twists: The conspiracy's true goal is NOT to assassinate the shōgun but to DISCREDIT him — flooding Edo with forged seals until his every decree is worthless and the great clans rise in revolt. It's a coup by counterfeit, not by blade.
Lady Kumohime is a true believer who sees herself as a liberator, not a villain — and a clever party can talk her into surrender rather than kill her, ending the plot through words instead of steel.

The forged coin and seals move through the city hidden in fish barrels at the dawn market, timed to the pre-dawn hour when the watch never patrols — the whole criminal supply line runs through the most public place in Edo.

The recovered master seal-die is as dangerous in the party's (or Hattori's) hands as in the clan's — whoever holds it can forge the warlord's word at will. The real moral test comes AFTER the villain is defeated: what do the heroes do with the weapon they captured?
dmTips: Lean hard into the setting's senses on every turn — lantern-light on wet timber, incense and grilled eel, the clack of geta sandals, the chirp of nightingale floors, fireworks over black rooftops. Edo should feel like a real, breathing city, and the culturalCodex gives you true details to layer in.

Honor the bathhouse and temple etiquette beats mechanically: players who observe the customs (washing before the bath, drawing fortunes respectfully, bowing in the ring) blend in and gain real advantages; players who blunder draw notice. This rewards engagement with the culture rather than just the combat.

The chase and rooftop scenes live or die on pacing — keep them fast, call for honest skill checks with real consequences (a fall, a lost step, a toppled stall) BEFORE the violence lands, and always declare fall-damage and DCs before the edge-roll. The fall is the deadliest enemy on the roofs; use it fairly and never fudge it.

The Oni's Regeneration is a puzzle, not a wall: telegraph through the Arcana clue and the flammable terrain that FIRE shuts off its healing. Don't fudge its HP — make the players solve it by setting the paper-stacked cellar alight. The spreading fire is then a hazard for everyone, including them.

The finale has a genuine non-combat resolution: a high-DC Persuasion (set up by an Insight read of Kumohime's real plot) lets a silver-tongued party take her alive without the oni fight. Award EQUAL XP for talking her down as for killing her — and let the players' choices about mercy and the master seal-die carry real, lasting weight. There is no single 'correct' ending, only the kind of heroes they chose to be.

Combat is honest and can be deadly at these levels — the Assassin and Oni are heavy hitters. Use the lighter stat substitutions noted in each encounter for a fair table, the heavier ones for a deadly table, and either way let the dice fall where they may. A TPK is a valid outcome; so is a clever surrender. Never invent phantom HP or a deus ex machina to rescue a party the dice have doomed.
